title: A rift in the sky
caption: The Great Rift above the VISTA telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Dark lanes cut across the brightest part of the Milky Way above ESO's VISTA telescope at Paranal Observatory, so that the glowing region seems to play hide-and-seek with the telescope. These dark lines are known as the Great Rift.

The Rift is made of vast clouds of gas and dust lying between the Solar System and the inner Milky Way. They soak up most of the visible light from the billions of stars at the centre of our galaxy. Yet astronomers can still study the inner Milky Way, because infrared and radio light pass through the clouds without being absorbed, letting telescopes effectively look through the Rift.

VISTA, the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy, stands on the peak next to the one holding the Very Large Telescope. It is one of the largest infrared survey telescopes, helping to map the Universe and study questions such as how galaxies evolve.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at an ESO site, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long exposure gathers more light than the eye, making the Milky Way's bright core and the dark dust lanes of the Great Rift stand out more strongly.

explore: Infrared telescopes such as VISTA are well suited to peering past dust. Where the eye and ordinary cameras see only darkness in the Rift, infrared light reveals the stars that lie hidden beyond.
alt: Dark dust lanes cross the bright band of the Milky Way above a telescope building on a mountain top.
